title: Born in Leipzig
description: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz is born in Leipzig, Saxony, two years before the Peace of Westphalia ends the Thirty Years' War. His father, Friedrich Leibnüzen, is professor of moral philosophy at Leipzig University.

title: Father's death; the library
description: Friedrich Leibniz dies when his son is six. The boy gains access to his father's library and, by his own account, teaches himself Latin and Greek from its shelves.

title: Enters Leipzig University
description: At fifteen, Leibniz enrolls in philosophy at Leipzig, reading scholastic texts alongside the new mechanical philosophy of Descartes, Hobbes, and Gassendi.

title: First book: On the Combinatorial Art
description: Publishes Dissertatio de arte combinatoria — his first statement of the idea that complex thoughts are compounds of simple symbols, the seed of the universal characteristic. Takes his doctorate in law at Altdorf and declines a professorship.

title: Enters the service of the Elector of Mainz
description: Works on legal reform, electoral policy, and schemes for a European confederation to secure peace after the wars of Louis XIV.

title: Diplomatic mission to Paris
description: Sent to Paris to distract Louis XIV from attacking the Netherlands. The plan fails; the stay transforms Leibniz. He meets Huygens, Malebranche, and Arnauld, and studies the mathematics of Descartes and Pascal.

title: Invents the calculus
description: Working alone in Paris, Leibniz develops the differential and integral calculus, including the d and ∫ notation still in use. He publishes the method in Acta Eruditorum in 1684.

title: Enters Hanover service
description: Accepts the post of counselor and librarian to Duke Johann Friedrich of Hanover — the start of a forty-year association with the Guelph court.

title: Harz mining engineering
description: Serves as mining engineer in the Harz mountains, designing wind-powered drainage schemes and writing on geology — his 'proto-evolutionary' claim that the earth once had a fluid past.

title: Discourse on Metaphysics
description: Composes the Discours de métaphysique and sends its summary to Antoine Arnauld. The resulting correspondence becomes one of the great documents of philosophy.

title: Travels for the Guelph history
description: Journeys through southern Germany, Austria, and Italy researching the genealogy of the House of Guelph, visiting mines, libraries, and academies en route.

title: The 'New System' published
description: Publishes the Système nouveau in the Journal des sçavans, presenting his doctrine of pre-established harmony to the European reading public and provoking decades of debate.

title: Founds the Berlin Academy
description: Leibniz becomes the first president of the new Brandenburg Society of Sciences (later the Prussian Academy), founded largely on his initiative and planning.

title: Théodicée
description: Publishes the Essais de Théodicée — his only major philosophical book to appear in his lifetime — defending divine justice and the claim that ours is the best of all possible worlds against Pierre Bayle.

title: Correspondence with Samuel Clarke
description: Exchanges letters with Newton's champion Samuel Clarke on space, time, and God — the last great metaphysical controversy of his life, cut short by his death.

title: Composes the Monadology
description: In Vienna, writes the ninety-paragraph summary of his philosophy (the Monadology, or Principes de la philosophie), which circulates only in manuscript and is not published until 1720, after his death.

title: Death in Hanover
description: Dies in Hanover aged seventy. The court ignores his passing; only his secretary attends the funeral. He leaves roughly a hundred thousand manuscript pages, still being edited today.

title: New Essays published
description: His Nouveaux essais sur l'entendement humain — a paragraph-by-paragraph answer to Locke, suppressed for fifty years after his death — finally appears in print.
